Herald decides whether a message is worth interrupting you for before a word of it is said. Each message carries an importance, the page sets a floor, and the engine returns a verdict.

We sent one at 80 against a floor of 50 and it was delivered: the 3D character in the corner of the page said it. We sent the next at 29. The character said nothing, and the verdict came back as a drop with its reason: below-importance-floor.

Every message that is not delivered comes back with a reason, so why you were not told has an answer.

three.ws/herald

A drop and a hold are different verdicts.

A held message is delivered once the thing blocking it clears: another message on screen, a tab in the background, a full rate limit, quiet hours. A dropped one is reported with its reason and will not be delivered.
A verdict of deliver is what makes the 3D character speak, with the gesture the sender chose. On a page with no GPU the same verdict arrives as a card, in a live region, dismissible with Escape.

To share a capture, add ?src= and the address of the file to the address of the viewer. The scene loads as the page opens, so the link is the whole handoff.

The same scene that is a 1 GB PLY is roughly 100 MB as SPZ.

posts.text:
An avatar manifest that carries the SHA-256 of the mesh it was built from, so a model re-exported or swapped under the same filename fails your build instead of your page.

The three-ws-avatar command reads the GLB once and writes its digest and size into the manifest, then validates the whole document against the published schema. Four commands, one runtime dependency, no network calls, so it runs offline inside a release script.

preview prints the two lines of HTML that embed the avatar. The page pastes them in unmodified, and the viewer on it is that markup rendering.

validate exits non-zero on an invalid manifest and prints each error at the path where it happened, so a bad file fails the build step instead of logging a warning. hash prints the digest alone on stdout, which makes the drift check a one-line comparison.

Install line, the four commands, and the manifest fields: three.ws/avatar-cli
The owner is a chain-scoped account, so ownership is unambiguous off-platform. A Solana address is accepted as is.

posts.text:
A checksum tells you two GLB files differ. It cannot tell a lossless re-export from a rig that quietly lost joints, and only one of those takes your avatar off the screen.

Model Diff reads both files and reports the change set: geometry, materials, textures, skeletons and animation clips, with renames and moves detected the way git detects them. Both files are parsed and compared in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.

In the reel, two different characters: the verdict is breaking, with 2 joints lost, 5 animations removed and 4 objects renamed rather than rewritten. three.ws/diff

Severity is one of none, cosmetic, minor, major, breaking, so a build can gate on it. Breaking means something a consumer references by name is gone: a clip, a joint, a mesh. That is the failure that renders fine and never moves.

Vertex data is compared at a quantum of 1e-4 units, so the float drift of a re-export does not register while a genuine edit does.

The same engine runs this page, the CLI and the free API, so a verdict in CI cannot disagree with what you see here. Hand the CLI two files and a --fail-on level, and the build fails on the severity you choose.

Gold, chrome, copper, glass, wood, stone, car paint, neon, holographic. Each one is a set of real PBR values (color, how metallic, how rough), so the model reflects light as you turn it instead of wearing a flat tint.

Your original is never touched, and Reset puts it back.

For a finish that is not on the list, describe it in plain words, like worn copper or glossy ceramic, and IBM Granite proposes the PBR values. They are applied live and saved as a new version, never over the one before it.

Then fine-tune how metallic and how rough it is with sliders and export a validated GLB.
The reel uses the platform's sample avatar, which loads by default when you bring no model. Drop in a .glb, or paste a public link to one, and every finish works the same way on it.
